extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers and practitioners in financial auditing (audit firms, compliance engineers) working on automated compliance verification with LLMs
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, prompting, and evaluating large language models to determine whether text passages from financial reports comply with regulatory accounting requirements (IFRS / HGB). Involves dataset annotation, prompt engineering, model selection, and class-level metric reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision, Recall, F1 (per-class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision(c) = |TP(c)| / (|TP(c)| + |FP(c)|), Recall(c) = |TP(c)| / (|TP(c)| + |FN(c)|), F1(c) = 2 * (Precision(c)*Recall(c)) / (Precision(c)+Recall(c)). Here c ∈ C represents the class (either “yes”, “no”, “unclear”, or “not applicable”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute precision, recall, and F1 for each predicted class; use these per-class scores to analyze model strengths and weaknesses (e.g., models may be overly confident in 'yes'/'no' and ignore 'unclear').

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro and Micro averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Macro average: unweighted mean of per-class recalls (Recall_macro = (1/|C|) Σ_i Recall(c_i)). Micro average: support-weighted mean over classes (Recall_micro = Σ_i |TP(c_i)| / Σ_i (|TP(c_i)| + |FN(c_i)|)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both macro and micro averages across classes (and across prompts) to capture class-balance-insensitive and support-weighted performance respectively; use micro F1 to compare overall model/prompt performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation label scheme (IFRS and HGB)
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRS: annotations labeled as 'yes', 'no', or 'unclear'. HGB: annotations labeled as 'yes', 'no', 'unclear', or 'not applicable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify label meanings to annotators (e.g., 'unclear' if insufficient context; 'not applicable' if requirement irrelevant). Use consistent label sets per jurisdiction/standard when evaluating models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset annotation & quality control process
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations were done by PwC auditors: three auditors split annotation work, overseen by a senior auditor; labels were verified and fine-tuned through several rounds of review and by re-examining random annotated samples and qualitatively assessing false positives and negatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain multi-annotator workflow with senior oversight, iterative review rounds, random sample re-checks, and qualitative error analysis to produce reliable ground truth for compliance evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation grouping and averaging procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: All scores are grouped by the prompt used to query a model and then averaged across the dataset to determine the overall performance per class. Averages across all classes use macro and micro averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing models, evaluate each model across all prompt variants, then report per-prompt averages and best-performing prompt for each model/dataset combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baselines / model selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Include multiple LLMs as baselines: open-source (Llama-2 7b, 13b, 70b) and proprietary (GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k, GPT-4). Rationale: economic considerations, data privacy, and fine-tuning potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare open-source and proprietary models across identical prompts and inference parameters; consider deployability trade-offs (cost, privacy, fine-tuning capability) when selecting models for production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt design factors: task phrasing and response structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Two key prompt factors: (1) task phrasing (how the task is presented, e.g., chain-of-thought, one-shot, Tree-of-Thought adaptations) and (2) permitted model response structure (open-ended explanations vs closed structured answers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with multiple phrasing techniques and response-structure constraints; the paper finds short prompts with examples and closed structured outputs often perform better than verbose CoT/TOT styles for this auditing task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response format: closed (JSON) vs open-ended
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed format constrains the model to return only 'yes', 'no', 'unclear' or 'not applicable' (often in a JSON schema). Open-ended allows explanations. The study observed that the 'closed' format yielded superior performance compared to 'open-ended'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce machine-readable structured outputs (e.g., JSON with an 'answer' field) to improve consistency and enable automated aggregation/parsing; prefer closed schemas for production pipelines where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deployment objective: minimize false positives (practical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In collaboration with auditors, the compliance check system should avoid false positive predictions at all costs. Detection of non-compliance ('No') is critical; the system should prioritize high precision and recall for the 'No' class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When optimizing models for deployment, tune toward conservative behavior that reduces false positives on compliance decisions (e.g., thresholding, calibration, human-in-the-loop verification for positives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language / dataset-specific evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate models separately for different reporting standards/languages (IFRS primarily English; HGB German). Note: many LLMs are trained mainly on English and perform worse on non-English datasets (observed poorer performance on HGB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess language coverage of chosen models and consider language-specific models or fine-tuning; treat cross-language performance gaps as a key deployment risk factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling verbose / inconsistent outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some models (e.g., Llama-2 variants) produced verbose outputs or inconsistent machine-readable outputs for some prompt formats, causing heuristics/parsers to fail and yielding zero scores for some configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prompts and output validation heuristics robust to verbosity; enforce strict output schemas; preprocess or constrain model outputs to ensure consistent parsing in evaluation and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling strategy for experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to dataset size, random sampling was used: IFRS dataset -> sampled 10 reports and sub-sampled 100 requirements; HGB dataset -> randomly selected 3 reports and requirements with at least two annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative random sampling while ensuring sufficient annotation density per requirement; report sampling procedure and any selection constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting per-model/per-prompt breakdowns (micro F1, best prompt identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report micro F1 scores per model and dataset for the best-performing prompt and averages over all prompts. Also report which prompt configuration was best per model/dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed tables showing per-model, per-prompt, per-dataset micro/macro scores and identify best-performing prompt templates to guide prompt selection for deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template I — In-Out-Sub-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple Yes/No/Unclear/Not applicable answer. Short, point-by-point answers without explanation. Formatting in JSON schema. Example: System instructs expert auditor persona and requests JSON: {'answer':<'yes'|'no'>}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for concise classification of sub-requirements; enforces compact machine-readable answers suitable for automated pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template II — Cot-Sub-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain-of-thought response leveraging intermediate explanations before the final answer. Specification of relevant line numbers from the document. No JSON schema formatting required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when wanting model internal reasoning traces and line references for human inspection; expect potentially lower raw classification performance and higher verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template III — In-Out-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplified version of In-Out-Sub. Direct Yes/No/Unclear/Not applicable response. Formatting in JSON schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for straightforward, compact classification without requiring sub-requirement decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template IV — Cot-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Step-by-step response and explanation for each sub-request; detailed explanation for each sub-request. No JSON schema formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitable for eliciting detailed rationales per sub-requirement; expect verbose responses and need for parsers/heuristics if extracting final labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template V — In-Out-Tot-Template (Tree-of-Thought adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Same as In-Out, with Tree-of-Thought prompting: imagine three experts giving stepwise thoughts and coming to a majority conclusion. Format output in JSON schema with a final 'answer'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to simulate multi-expert deliberation within a single prompt; computationally heavier in traditional TOT but here adapted into single-prompt style; may or may not improve performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template VI — In-Out-Tot-One-Shot-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Same as In-Out-Tot, with the addition of a one-shot example (chosen example shows compliance). Includes multi-expert stepwise thinking and a final JSON answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding a one-shot positive example can help model calibration toward the desired output format and decision; helpful when few exemplar cases are representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template VII — In-Out-One-Shot-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Same as In-Out with addition of a one-shot example where the text passage complies with the requirement. Enforces JSON formatted answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise example to show desired labeling behavior and output schema; can improve consistency and reduce parser errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt template VIII — In-Out-One-Shot-No-Template
rubrics_metrics.description: Same as In-Out with a one-shot example where the chosen example does NOT comply with the requirement. Enforces JSON formatted answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide negative example to demonstrate how to label non-compliance; useful for balancing examples across classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: German-language prompt templates and label expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: German variants of the templates I–VIII instruct an expert with perfect knowledge of the HGB standard. They explicitly support answers: 'yes', 'no', 'unclear', and 'not applicable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with German/HGB data, use language-appropriate prompts and include the expanded label set; account for LLMs' weaker German proficiency in selection/fine-tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical finding: short prompts + example often beat advanced prompting
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation: prompt I ('In-Out-Sub-Template') achieved the best score in 4 out of 12 model/dataset cases; brief prompts paired with exemplary one-shot instructions can improve response quality. Advanced techniques (CoT, TOT) did not consistently outperform simpler prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experimenting with brief, example-backed prompts before investing in costly multi-step prompting strategies; measure per-model/prompt performance rather than assuming more complex prompting helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure modes reporting (class-specific blindspots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed failure modes: models often failed to detect the 'unclear' class (tended to be overconfident in 'yes'/'no'); some models performed significantly worse on German HGB data; larger parameter size did not always imply better performance (Llama-2-70b sometimes worse than 7b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-class confusion patterns and be cautious extrapolating from parameter count to real-world performance; include checks for overconfidence and class-coverage gaps.
